author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Jamaica is petitioning the British king to refer three questions about the Transatlantic slave trade to a London court. Was the enslavement of Africans unlawful under English law at the time? Does it constitute crimes against humanity under international law? Does Britain therefore have a legal obligation to provide redress? Jamaica hopes the answers could establish a legal basis for reparations. This campaign is part of a broader push for countries to pay for their roles in the Transatlantic slave trade. A UN committee said last month that governments are obliged by law to consider paying damages. 
Presenter: Dareen Abughaida
Guests:
Hilary Beckles - Chairman of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission and Vice Chancellor of the University of the West Indies. 
Lawrence Goldman - Emeritus Fellow in History at St Peter's College, University of Oxford, and former Editor of the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography.

Every night at 11:18pm, the exact moment of the deadly 2023 Tempe train crash, families of the victims gather outside the Greek Parliament to read the names of the 57 passengers who died. Panos stands among them, mourning his 23-year-old son, Dennis.

Three years on, authorities have yet to fully account for what happened. As allegations of safety failures and missing evidence mount, anger among the families deepens. With the long-awaited trial into the crash approaching, Panos emerges as one of the leading figures of the protest movement, demanding accountability for the devastating crash.

The Tempe 57 is a documentary film by Anna Prokou and Nina Maria Pashalidou.


#documentary #aljazeeraenglish #Greece #TempeTrainCrash #Witnessdocumentary
title: Greece’s deadliest train crash: A father's search for answers three years on | Witness Documentary

author: Al Jazeera English
description: It's nearly a month since Israeli settlers began to lay siege to several homes in the village of Qusra, in the occupied West Bank — part of an effort to force Palestinians from their land. Four-year-old Kinda is trapped in one of those homes, missing the start of her first year of school. Her aunt said: "The girls have many questions. Why are we still here? Why can't we go out or have people visit us? Any sound they hear outside gets them worried and scared." What started as a siege by Israeli settlers has now turned into a closed military zone, with Israeli soldiers present and military gates established near the besieged homes. Kinda's teacher is also missing the beginning of the school year, joining her students online. Israeli settler attacks are averaging six per day, according to the UN, alongside a surge in illegal settlement outposts. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army to dismantle some illegal structures in response to US pressure, but outposts dismantled
title: Palestinian child misses first day of school as family remains trapped under Qusra settler siege

Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held a joint press conference in Moscow, addressing regional tensions and bilateral relations. Prince Faisal condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure, calling them a "blatant violation" of international law and a threat to regional security. He warned that the Houthis' "selfishness will lead to results that cannot be bearable", while reaffirming that Saudi Arabia "will never hesitate to defend itself" but remains committed to diplomacy. Lavrov said Western powers were responsible for the roots of the Ukraine conflict, accusing the European Union of blocking efforts to address its "deep roots". Both ministers discussed expanding the Saudi-Russian strategic partnership across investment, trade and culture, and explored regional security initiatives involving Gulf countries, Iraq, Jordan and UN Security Council members.

description: Qatar's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Ibrahim Al Hashmi has given his weekly briefing in Doha, covering a series of diplomatic engagements. author: Al Jazeera English
description:
In northeastern Syria, more than 2,300 women and children are imprisoned in Roj camp as relatives of suspected ISIL fighters and people linked to the armed group. 
Government sources have told Al Jazeera that their home countries are deliberately ignoring them. Damascus wants to close the camp, but rights groups have called it a "ticking time bomb", where many detainees are vulnerable to the influence of a handful of women linked to ISIL. 
There are about 50 nationalities represented in the camp, including American, Swiss, British, Italian, Belgian, Turkish, Russian, Chinese and Bosnian. 
One woman from Sarajevo said: "We are full of the trauma. We lost any hope. We are just waiting to go home." The women interviewed have not been charged with a crime or given the opportunity to present their case in a court of law. 

Al Jazeera's Bernard Smith sent this exclusive report from Roj camp in northeastern Syria.

Saudi authorities say Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, officially known as Ansar Allah, have carried out attacks on energy facilities in the south of the kingdom, wounding at least 73 civilians, including women and children. 
The Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said the attacks hit civilian and economic sites in Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran, calling it a "dangerous escalation" and a "blatant violation" of Saudi sovereignty. 
He warned the coalition would take "all necessary operational measures". 
Saudi political analyst Khaled Batarfi told Al Jazeera the escalation is "too much" and expects the coalition to respond "eye for an eye". 
The attacks come as fighting intensifies in Yemen, where government-aligned forces have launched a counteroffensive against Houthi positions. 
The World Health Organization says 1,078 people have been killed or wounded since August 24, while more than 21,000 have been displaced since Thursday.

description: Canada is imposing counter-tariffs ranging from 15 to 50 percent on nearly $20bn worth of US imports, matching US levies on Canadian goods including machinery, textiles and consumer products. The dispute began with Donald Trump's return to office, when he imposed tariffs on Canadian imports and threatened further action, while also raising the prospect of Canada becoming the 51st US state. Canada has responded with its own tariffs and is exploring alternative trading partners, including the European Union and China.
